title: Essence
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of this Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating kindness and warmth towards oneself and one's body as the essence of true practice. This involves recognizing that our nature is already tranquil and imperturbable, and that we can develop a deeper understanding of ourselves and the world by embracing silence and letting go of external expectations or desires. By doing so, we can transform our lives and share this tranquility with others, living in harmony with the world rather than isolating ourselves from it.

sentences.text: Well, first I want to remember to say a few thank-yous, most immediately thank you for being here.
Maybe the only real choice we have is where we put our body at one time, right?
It unfolds from there.
If your body's not there, nothing's happening there.
So you chose to put your body here, so that's pretty great, I think.
I hope you think so, too.
And I want to thank everybody also for all the wonderful birthday wishes.
A lot of us came to different parts of the party, though not everyone could come.
The sangha gave me a wonderful gift of calligraphy supplies, so that'll encourage me to keep practicing my calligraphy.
And my cousin sent up a beautiful drum, so that encourages me to play the drum.
So it seems like the presents are suggesting that it'd be good if I cultivated my creative side.
Nobody sent me a new computer or "how to get things done" books or anything like that.
Actually, back to today, I want to especially thank Connie and Talus and Bob, the primary architects of how this could happen.
Uh-oh, and I wouldn't have thought about my birthday, actually.
I haven't looked this up, but I suspect that for a very high percentage of human history, life expectancy was less than 50 years.
Does that seem like that's probably true?
Yeah.
So I'm just remembering this morning how lucky that is.
Wow.
What a blessing to be still alive.
And of course, I'm younger than most of you, so...
It's not true anymore, I guess, so much, but it used to be I was usually the youngest one in the Zendo.
So it's good that that's not totally true anymore.
Where would things be going if the youngest one was 50?
So anyway, we go on for another year.
Let's see what happens and where we put our body.
We're especially being curious for practice period this year about our first Zen ancestors in the West.
What were they trying to do?
What were they trying to bring us?
What were their intentions?
I thought about this a little bit and kept coming back to two connected ideas: form and essence.
Today we're experimenting with a certain form, our version of the Soto Zen monastic form for a day.
For the day we're creating a little monastery, one of many Soto Zen forms, it turns out.
We're trying to do this really thoroughly and take it very seriously.
It's complicated, and people had to do a lot of work, and are making a lot of effort, to constellate this monastic form.
So let's really do that.
Each of us is in the matrix of this form.
It's not like the leaders create something and then we are just hanging around in the middle.
We're all co-creating this all day today.
So let's do this fully, as Connie said so beautifully this morning.
Let's take this seriously.
Being careful how we move this body around, how we hold this body for the day.
Dropping deeply into our breath and our body, moment after moment, moving around in an upright, dignified way.
Very important, how we move.
Not stuffy, but upright.
Because the form really holds us if we let it.
Really protects us.
But it can only function if we give ourselves to it fully.
And for all of us to function together, this form requires a lot of trust.
A lot of letting go, probably a lot of forgiveness.
A certain kind of effort and energy that's really kind of subtle.
That's a key point to what we're doing in bringing forward this form.
But what is the essence of this?
What is the purpose of all this?

Did these Japanese Zen priests and Westerners who went over to Japan to train just have this compelling idea that it would be really super awesome and special if Americans put on special clothes and acted in a certain way and created certain kinds of buildings?
So they wouldn't be homesick or something like that?
Is it just the form that they were transmitting?
Of course we don't think so.
We think there must be something to this.
So here are a few words from Suzuki Roshi, maybe a little bit about the essence of what he was trying to offer people.
Now, reflected in his books and the expressions that get repeated, the stories that get told, we think of Suzuki Roshi as very fluid and free and very much about essence.
But actually, he was the leader of the first Buddhist monastery in the Western Hemisphere, with very strict rules, very strong form.
So clearly both were going on.
This is an excerpt from the *Not Always So* book.
They took all of his talks that got recorded on scratchy cassette tapes, and made them into a couple of books with a lot of editing.
Suzuki Roshi said something like:
*I want you to have the actual feeling of true practice.
Because even though I practiced zazen when I was young, I didn't know exactly what it was.
Sometimes I was very impressed by our practice at Eiheiji,* the big monastery he went to, *and other temples.
When I saw great teachers who listened to their lectures, I was deeply moved.
But it was difficult to understand.
Our aim is to have complete experience or full feeling in each moment of practice.*
*What we teach is that enlightenment and practice are one.
But my practice was what we call* stepladder practice.
*I'll understand this much now, and then next year I thought I'll understand a little bit more, like climbing up a step ladder.
That kind of practice doesn't make much sense because I could never be satisfied.
If you try step ladder practice, maybe you too will realize this is a mistake.
If we do not have a warm, big satisfaction in our practice, this is not true practice.
Even though you sit trying to have the right posture and counting your breath, it may be lifeless practice, lifeless zazen.
Because you're just following instructions.
You're not kind enough with yourself.*
Did you see that coming?
Kind enough with yourself.
Not what most people think of when they hear about Zen.
Kind?
*Kind enough with yourself.
You think that if you follow the instructions given by some teacher, you will have good zazen.
But the purpose of instruction is to encourage you to be kind to yourself.
Do not count your breath just to avoid your thinking mind, but to take the best care of your breathing.
If you're kind with your breathing one breath after another, you will have a refined, refreshed, warm feeling in your zazen.
When you have a warm feeling for your body and your breath, then you can take care of your practice and be fully satisfied.
When you're very kind with yourself, naturally you will feel like this.*
The essence involves kindness.
The kindness within a very particular way of living, way of being.
So, the actual feeling of true practice.
As we said first, I want you to understand the actual feeling of true practice.
Is that something that we feel when everything goes really great?
Really smoothly?
Everybody thanks us for a wonderful retreat.
What a warm, loving sangha we are.
Is this sense of the true, actual feeling of practice dependent on some particular result from the form?
Like it's working?
Or do we learn about the actual feeling of true practice when our edges get rubbed a little bit and things don't go so smoothly?
And what if we can't feel it at all?
What if we say, what?
There is no actual feeling of true practice here.
Maybe I shouldn't have come today.
I'm trying to say it the way you said it.
The actual feeling of true practice, then.
That's something I think really to think about and to notice.
Is whatever the essence is contingent or dependent on some particular result or circumstance that you like?
Maybe you think, oh, but this is not just the usual kind of grabby liking.
This is my subtle spiritual liking.
But is that really indifferent?

As you know from the earlier talks, or maybe you're just hearing this so I'll sketch it briefly, Suzuki Roshi was sent by the Japanese Soto establishment, by the church, in the 50s to work with an immigrant church in San Francisco.
And then pretty soon American people of the 60s got excited about Zen masters and meditation and stuff.
And then pretty soon he needed some help.
In parallel to his story, another priest, a somewhat younger priest named Dainin Katagiri, was in America.
He was sent to work with a Japanese congregation in Los Angeles.

And through mysterious circumstances (I shared with you that I read a pretty long biography of Katagiri Roshi, and they glossed over this part, which is interesting), somehow he left that job, left Los Angeles, which was a very big no-no.
He was just going to live independently in San Francisco.
I don't even know what his green card status was or something like that.
So Katagiri, this young Japanese priest, liked Suzuki, and was very excited about the English language and Western life and a sense of freshness to it all from their point of view.
He was hanging around in San Francisco.
He was going to go to college and he was interested in making art, actually.
He wanted to be a sculptor.
But Suzuki Roshi got a hold of him and he had to go help.
There's an interesting little part; you can listen to the other talk about that.
He was reluctant.
He didn't really want to do it, but he realized he'd been asked.
He'd been asked in a way that he had to say yes and embrace it.
So form showed up for him.
He got interested in another kind of form, a free Western life form.
The next thing he knew he was at the first Buddhist monastery in the Western Hemisphere, right back to Eiheiji.
So anyway, he's talking about this point a little sometime later with his students in Minnesota, where he ended up starting an important center.
What he's suggesting is that we need faith, actually, for all this to work.
This actual feeling of true practice can't be just something like cause and result, cause and effect, that we notice with our conscious mind.
He says a piece of this is faith.
We associate faith with the theistic tradition, so maybe you don't like that word or maybe you love that word.
Finally, we get faith here.
I don't know.
Either way would not be right.
He could substitute trust if you want, but anyway, he said faith.
So Katagiri said:
*According to Dogen Zenji's understanding of faith, there is nothing that persuades us or pushes us or forces us to create faith.
Faith means tranquility.
And complete tranquility is the source of our nature and our existence.
There is no need to talk about tranquility or not tranquility in our life or in our Zazen.
Everybody is already perfectly tranquil.*
He's talking about you.
*Everybody is already perfectly tranquil.
That is why people who do not practice Buddhism seem to seek for tranquility.
And in actuality, they seek for it and struggle for it in many ways.
They work hard during the day and they just want to come back to their home and sit down and relax.
Regardless of whether that house is fancy or not or messy or clean, we should always be mindful of our original nature that is perfectly tranquil.
Because daily life becomes so busy, we may forget it or ignore it.
We should trust in this tranquility and practice it within the original nature of tranquility.*
There's a lot there.
We should trust in this tranquility, practice it, and practice it within its nature, within the original nature of tranquility.
*Then we will be able to improve greatly in the practice of tranquility.*
So this is the basic dialectic of our school.
Have faith.
It's already there.
You don't need to do anything.
And then you can practice.
And you have to practice, right?
You have to practice.
*And it will improve us.
But if we behave in a certain manner, so as to let this imperturbability break forth, if we behave in a certain manner, so as to let the imperturbability break forth, it will really come up.
If we do not behave in such a way, we will never have a chance to know, to realize the imperturbability we already have.
We already have.
Zazen is to adjust our body and mind to exactly fit this imperturbability, so it naturally comes up.
Zazen is exactly identical with the original nature of existence, which is called tranquility, called imperturbability.*
So you can see that this is deliberately frustrating our little mind, right?
It's not this leads to that, it's not that leads to this.
Somehow it's faith in this allows that, that reflects back on this and allows this to be that and that to be this, and so on and so on and so on.
Imperturbability breaks forth.
So, essence arising from form, if we let it.
If we're present and participating, if we have faith and commitment, if we're pretty darn patient.
This morning I was feeling a little bit like maybe we haven't emphasized quite enough around here how important sesshin practice is.
Buddha really emphasized this, actually.
He didn't call it that because it wasn't Japanese, but there's a real value to having some times where everything is really set aside.
His basic recommendation was that the right amount of time would be your entire lifetime.
That would be the right amount of time.
Quit your job, leave your family, become a monastic.
Practice like a sesshin schedule every day for the rest of your life.
We want to make Buddhism accessible, which is wonderful, and of course I'm doing that all the time.
So we're also emphasizing the true fact that all this functions completely in our ordinary lives as well.
Form and essence.
We don't have to be monastics.
Within our ordinary lay life we can practice deeply and be transformed and transform our world.
And we say everything is practice, right?
Everything is practice, and that's really true.
But kind of like Katagiri was saying, it's also true that we need monastic practice.
So it's beautiful that we're here today with our bodies, actualizing that.
For sesshin day we take this on for this day, maybe another time for a week.
Maybe another time we can clear our schedule to go to a bigger center where they can support us to be in the quiet container of practice for a month or three months or a year.
It's part of what we need to do.
It's part of our heritage, part of our obligation.
And it's wonderful.
It's a wonderful obligation.
It's a joyous obligation.
Not always so easy to do.
And it may at times seem just silly how complex it is.
Connie is in the epicenter of that complexity today, the eye of the storm.
She has a clipboard with a mini piece of paper on it, to enable all of us to just let go of everything.
One breath.
One breath is supported by a very thick clipboard.
And part of our training here is to have to carry the clipboard.
To rotate our roles, to tangle with where to clack and when to ring, and to have it be a little more busy than we want.
And that's okay, because that's how this imperturbability can break forth.
And I was also appreciating with Chris recently how she's leading us in offering some quiet days with fewer forms.
She decided to call, or maybe I thought of this to call, simple sit.
So this is good too, different ways of expressing this.
And of course not everybody can be here.
Apparently not everybody's here today.
And so we need to sit for them too.
To practice deeply for the benefit of everyone else in the Sangha, and everyone else we know, including the people who are never going to come to this kind of thing.
Ever.
And it's not our job to talk them into it either.
I didn't look it up but it made me think of another famous Suzuki Roshi expression.
In the early days of San Francisco Zen Center, the way I've heard it told, there was an ungodly amount of enthusiasm.
If we'd been sucked into it, we wouldn't have noticed.
But if we'd been there and not sucked into it, we would have been completely blown away: holy smokes, these people are enthusiastic.
It was unbelievable.
Sit, sit, sit, sit.
We're changing the world, we're changing ourselves, we're changing everything.

And in the early Sangha, and I think this was probably the group in Los Altos, where most of the talks in Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind were recorded, not at big sesshins at Tassajara or something like that, but at informal gatherings in somebody's living room.
One time somebody was expressing how grouchy he or she was that their spouse was not coming.
"I got up, I got down to Red Cedar before 6 a.m., and where's my lazy spouse?"
Suzuki Roshi actually would get angry.
We don't always talk about this, but he got a little peeved.
In a very strong way he said, "That is wrong understanding.
Your spouse in bed is sitting side by side much better than you."
Something like that.
Not "okay, here's how to convince your spouse how important this is, blah, blah, blah."
So let's notice if the mind thinks of various people who should be here today, and remember Suzuki Roshi: no, no, no, they're doing much better Zazen than you somewhere else.
But it's wonderful that we're here doing the obvious Zazen.
Katagiri continues.
*There's a Zazen story that talks about this.
The 17th ancestor was walking around with his disciple, asking about the wind bells suspended from the four corners of the temple roof.
The teacher said, it's ringing.
Now the teacher asked the student, what is ringing?
The wind or the bells?*
What's ringing, the wind or the bells?
What would you say?
Of course the disciple knew this was a Zen question, so he said:
*The wind is not ringing, the bells are not ringing, the mind is ringing.
The wind is not ringing, the bells are not ringing, the mind is ringing.*
Katagiri says, *this is really true.
What is ringing?
The wind or the bells or both?
Whatever we say, it doesn't hit the mark.
So finally we try to find a solution.
But the mind is ringing.
This is very true, but still there's a question.
What is the mind?
What is this mind that's ringing?
To this question the disciple replied, tranquility, imperturbability.
The mind is vast, nothing to say, this is the original nature of existence.
In bells, in wind, in human beings, our mind, whatever it is.*
But then Dogen Zenji had an interesting comment about this story.
He said:
*It is the wind ringing, it is the chimes ringing, it is the blowing ringing, it is the ringing ringing, it is the ringing ringing.
Ringing ringing means the ringing entrusts itself to ringing, settles itself in ringing, and manifests itself in creative activity.
At that moment, ringing is all pervading without any obstructions.*
It's the ringing ringing.
What's amazing about being able to explore this stuff now, which wasn't true when these guys were talking, is that all the materials they were citing are now available in English.
So I was able to pretty easily look up what writing, what teaching the Katagiri was referring to in the 70s or 80s or whenever he said this.
He was quoting from a chapter of Shobogenzo, Dogen's great work of essays, called Emo, Emo, which means thusness, thusness.
Dogen was famous for starting with a sort of conventional way a story is thought about in Buddhism, just like Katagiri did there.
It's not the bell, it's not the wind, it must be the mind.
Yes, okay, good, good.
We should understand that everything is mediated by the mind, right?
We don't even really know exactly if there's wind or bells.
It's all perception in mind.
But then Dogen says, yeah, not far enough, not thorough enough.
So here's what Katagiri is quoting from in Dogen, as translated by Kaz Tanahashi and Peter Levitt.
*Saganandi, the 17th ancestor, acquired his Dharma heir, Gayashata, in the following way.
Hearing the wind bell ringing outside the hall, he asked Gayashata, is it the wind or the bell that is ringing?
Gayashata said, neither the wind nor the bell, it is the mind ringing.
Saganandi, the teacher, asked, what is this mind?
Gayashata said, altogether serene, altogether serene.
Saganandi said, splendid, splendid, who other than you will succeed me in my path?
Thus the treasury of the true Dharma eye was transmitted to Gayashata.*
So this is a famous trope, the transmission story.
Wouldn't that be fun?
The teacher asks you a question and somehow you come up with a really great answer and the teacher says, splendid, splendid, you will surely succeed me.
This hasn't happened yet for me, anyway.
But Dogen isn't satisfied.
Dogen goes on and says:
*This is the study that the mind is ringing while the wind is not ringing.
This is the study that the mind is ringing while the bell is not ringing.
Even if the mind ringing is thus, it is altogether serene.
This story was transmitted from India to China and has been regarded as a standard for study of the way.
But many have misunderstood it as follows.
Gayashata's statement, neither the wind nor the bell, it is the mind ringing, means that the very moment of listening, a thought arises.
The arising of a thought is called mind.
Without this mind thought, how can one relate to the sound of the bell ringing?
Because listening manifests with this thought, it should be regarded as the root of listening.
Therefore, Gayashata said, it's the mind ringing.*
So he set us up: okay, yeah, you agree, right?
I agree.
And Dogen says:
*This is wrong.
This is the wrong view.
They say this because they have not acquired the true power of authentic teaching.
This is like an interpretation by commentators in linguistics.
It is not the deep study of the Buddha way.*
In other words, it's just the surface, it's just the words.
Dogen continues:

*On the other hand, those who have studied with authentic heirs of the Buddha way take up unsurpassable enlightenment, the treasury of the true Dharma eye, and call it serene, non-doing, samadhi or dharani.
The meaning of this is that when even one single thing is serene, myriad things are serene.
If the blowing of the wind is serene, the ringing of the bell is serene.
That is why Gayashata said, altogether serene.
You may say the mind that is ringing is not the wind ringing.
The mind that is ringing is not the bell ringing.
The mind that is ringing is not the mind that is ringing.
Investigate thusness intimately and just say, the wind rings, the bell rings, the blowing rings, the ringing rings.
You realize thusness.*
Not because why be worried about thusness, but because why pursue thusness.
Thusness is a Buddhist term.
This is the translation of the Sanskrit ta-ta-ha-ta, ta-ta, ta-ta, ta-ta.
You can hardly say that, ta-ta.
It points to a kind of reality that we all know.
This is not a mysterious thing, though we so easily lose the thread of it, lose the feeling of the just coming together of it all, the just is-ness of each moment of our life.
Just this moment.
There's a depth and a radicalness to this that is like liberation itself, is the way it's thought about.
And so one of the names for the Buddha that we often say, ta-ta-ga-ta, is about this, about this just being thus, the one who is just thus.
In sesshin, the path to understanding this is fully inhabiting the silent container of our practice.
We do offer a talk in the middle just for entertainment, maybe a little distraction from your knee pain, maybe planting some seeds in your nose, maybe some feeling comes across, I don't know.
And of course listening to the talk is like zazen too.
But really we want to study this in every moment for the rest of the day.
Each moment of zazen, kinhin, cleaning, flipping through our clipboard, moving around the room.
Study this as we rest our awareness softly and gently in the breath, in the body.
Study this as we allow some of our self-concern and judgment and prickliness to relax a little bit, even as we allow it to manifest, because it too is part of thusness.
And this is why the practice of silence is so important.
It will be interesting for the rest of the day to support each other in dropping a little more fully into silence.
To study silence we also need to study what pulls us out of silence.
And this is different for each of us.
What emerges that pulls you out of silence?
Desire for a certain kind of connection or validation or expression or some result, something being one way or some other way.
So let's please notice what it is for each of us.
And even if we're in a situation where some degree of speaking is needed as part of our practice of silence, let's remember that that is also this practice of thusness.
Can we speak just the right words as best we can that are needed?
Can we speak them quietly?
Can we go close to the person and say just enough, or maybe just a gesture is enough?
Can we also be quiet in our gaze, in our body language, in our interactions?
Not as a repression or a holding something in, but as an expression of all this.
An expression of Buddha, an expression of this tranquility.
But these aren't rules to limit us or challenge us or make anything harder, but part of the form, part of the opportunity, part of the container by which the essence can spring forth.
Dogen said in there, *when even one single thing is serene, a myriad things are serene.
The blowing of the wind is serene, the ringing of the bell is serene.* All together serene.
If you are serene, I am serene.
Thank you, thank you.
And by the way, when Katagiri says imperturbable, I'm sure that they were translating the same word as serene.
Katagiri goes on to say that, although we need to train in the monastic container like we are today, then we open to the world.
Opening and closing, opening and closing, flapping our wings in some way.
*Tranquility does not mean inactivity.
Tranquility is not something we should hold onto by keeping away from human society.
It must be something alive in our life.
If we are completely isolated from human society, wherever we may go, our life does not work.
Going to live in the heart of the mountain seems like a way to have tranquility.
There it seems that we could handle our objects, our circumstances as we like, but actually we cannot.
If the tranquility we have is not expressed in our daily living, that tranquility is isolated and limited.
Accordingly, it results in a lack of sharing with others.*
So this kind of tranquility is something we can include others in.
*We just want to keep it to ourselves because it is nice.
If we stay at our home, it seems to be nice because nobody is interrupting us, but it's really just like a frog swimming in a very small well.
It's not the real state of human life.
It's trapped in the bottom of the well.
Tranquility must be backed by the unconditioned.
The unconditioned means purity, joy, peace, and also non-regression in our daily life.* Non-regression, not turning back, not turning back.
I looked up the word serious in the dictionary.
I noticed Connie used that word this morning.
It's a good word.
There are three principal definitions, and the first one is a little grim.
The synonyms for the first one are solemn, earnest, grave, unsmiling, and dour.
But the synonyms for the second definition are maybe more helpful for us: earnest, sincere, wholehearted, and genuine.
The last thing I want to quote is Dogen, who goes on later in this essay to talk about how we help each other.
How do we help each other manifest this wholehearted sincerity?
And how do we together encounter this essence of our practice?
He said:
*This kind of wisdom can neither be acquired from someone else nor aroused by oneself.
Wisdom is transmitted to wisdom.
Wisdom searches for wisdom.
Once, wisdom formed the bodies of 500 bats.
Listen to the Dharma.*
I'm not sure what story he's referring to.
*They had no other bodies and minds.
They were only bats.
At another time, wisdom was intimate within the bodies of 10,000 fish.
Even without conditions or causes, they could immediately attain understanding upon hearing the Dharma.
Wisdom neither comes nor enters.
It is just like when the god of spring encounters spring.
Wisdom is neither with thought nor without thought.
Wisdom is neither with mind nor without mind.
How can it be concerned with large or small?
How can it be discussed as delusion or enlightenment?
It means that without knowing what Buddha Dharma is, without having heard of it, one does not look for it and wish for it.
But upon hearing Dharma, one regards obligations as less weighty and forgets about oneself.
It is because the body and mind that has wisdom is no longer the self.
This is called, you trust and understand what you hear immediately.*
That's in italics.
It's probably a phrase from somewhere else.
I didn't look it up.
"Spring" there is like the season.
So it's not from someone else, and it's not just from ourself.
The implication is that it's both and neither.
We need ourself and we need each other.
Wisdom supports wisdom.
Wisdom searches for wisdom.
Wisdom manifests as wisdom.
And then the kicker here is so direct, actually.
We think of Dogen as pretty obscure, but this is very direct: *upon hearing the Dharma, one regards obligations as less weighty and forgets about oneself.* Forgets about oneself.
In the Vipassana community they talk about selfing.
Selfing.
To notice the suffering that comes with selfing.
And our quiet sesshin container is such a great opportunity to notice the wisdom that's letting go of the self and the selfing that arises.
So let's practice well for the rest of the day.
Practice quietly.
We will have an interesting sort of question for ourselves later in the day.
The way we ended up deciding to do this retreat, as with most of our in-town retreats, for the health and well-being of the kitchen and all of us, is that we don't provide an Oryoki dinner.
So there's a dinner break.
You can choose at that point whether you want to have a quiet meal with friends, with a conversation.
But maybe that conversation can be somehow in the spirit; you can experiment with that.
Or maybe you'll choose to maintain the silence in a more formal way, scrounging downstairs for leftovers.
Baba will let us know later if there's leftovers.
Or getting some deli food at the co-op and coming back here to eat quietly.
Whichever way you choose, wisdom will take care of itself.
You don't have to worry too much.
But we have bodies and we make choices.
We have a breath and we have this moment.
So dear friends in the Dharma, where's your breath right now?
What's the feeling of thusness in your heart now?
Is it the wind?
Is it the bell?
Is it the mind that's ringing?
Can we open to the beautiful nature of ringing itself?
The ringing is ringing.
Our heart is our heart.
We're okay as we are.
And today we have a wonderful opportunity, really rare.
This is hard to do.
Hard to create and offer and receive and show up.
You could've done all kinds of different things today.
You chose to be here.
We all chose to be here.
And what can we do but love each other and practice for the rest of the day.
So let's remember that as deeply as we can and continue.
Thank you very much.
